# Guardian Ring claim audit — 10/07/2026

## Result and scope

The inventory covers 959 stable claim keys and every distinct displayed value across 96 scenario combinations, all ten levels and three layers, assembly/component narration, cinematic lesson narration, and numeric/because text from all six built HTML pages. Duplicate values and narration are grouped, with their locations retained. Source dates, document page numbers, model names (TIRS-2), UI counts and keyboard shortcuts are included in the page inventory so they cannot be confused with measured hardware properties. Canvas values are covered through their pure model and lesson assumptions; this is not an OCR audit.

“Confirmed” means the stated evidence trail and scoped interpretation were checked, using the existing quoted research ledgers, the calculation tests below, or direct page inspection. It does not mean every external source was newly fetched or that every modeled claim is a measurement. “Footnoted” identifies an explicit existing illustration/teaching assumption or unavailable input. “Fixed” identifies changes in this branch.

## Fixes

- Fixed: the Kepler solver subtracted nearly equal terms and stopped against an absolute angular epsilon. For eccentricity 0.999999999999 and true eccentric anomaly 1e-6, the prior solution erred by about 5.04e-5 relative. It now evaluates a small-angle residual and derivative without cancellation and stops on relative progress. A constructed inverse regression failed before the fix and passes afterward. Ordinary displayed orbit values are unchanged at their stated precision.
- Fixed: ideal prime-focus and scan-reflection lessons were labeled Calc. in their dialogs but absent from the shared registry. Both now have calculation definitions and entries, backed by their geometric tests and the NASA reflection reference.
- Fixed: the claims gate previously checked only the generated combined research ledger. It now checks all seven canonical ledgers and rejects stale, missing or duplicated combined facts.
- Fixed after independent review: the DOM collector retains sentences containing inline evidence buttons. Every page row now needs an exact reviewed text, location, links and registry-key record in page-claim-reviews.json; missing or changed records are unreviewed and make this command fail. A synthetic unsupported numeric/because sentence verifies the actual command exits nonzero.
- Confirmed: the 1.22 diffraction coefficient is a rounded Airy coefficient, not an exact constant; an independent Bessel root confirms its rounding error is below 0.03%. No extra precision is attributed to it.

## Source review

The existing quoted source ledgers are [physics-review](physics-review.md), [spacecraft-review](spacecraft-review.md), [component review](COMPREHENSIVE-SYSTEMS-REVIEW.md), [TIRS-2 review](tirs2-architecture-review.md), [integration review](instrument-integration-review.md), [systems notes](systems/source-notes.md), and the design-practices fact/quote ledgers. Each cited entry below retains its exact source location. Unchecked sources remain excluded by the strict validator. Civil numbers stay attached to ABI, GOES-R or TIRS-2; assumed geometry never becomes military performance.

Fresh primary-source spot checks on 10/07/2026 confirmed NIST c/h/k, JPL Earth GM, NASA TIRS-2 43 K and 185 K design temperatures, NOAA ABI channels/cadences, and NASA reflection/prime-focus principles. These checks supplement the existing source review, rather than silently redate it.

- [NIST constants](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants/Table/allascii.txt): exact SI constants used by the tests and model.
- [JPL parameters](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/astro_par.html): Earth GM 398600.435507 km³/s².
- [NASA TIRS-2](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/landsat/tirs-2-testing-a-landsat-9-instrument-takes-shape/): named civil design temperatures, not generic detector settings.
- [NOAA ABI](https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/our-satellites/currently-flying/goes-east-west/advanced-baseline-imager-abi): named civil channel and imaging cadence facts.
- [NASA reflection](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter6-5/): Reflection section; equal angles and on-axis prime focus.

## Independent calculation checks

All paths below are in src/model. Relative-error assertions protect quantities with different scales; no fixed epsilon is used to accept tiny photon energies. Existing optics tests compare independently constructed geometric invariants.

| orbit-period | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: differentiated ellipse / polygon swept area; orbits.test.ts: reference period and scaling |
| orbit-speed | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: central-difference velocity from independently propagated positions |
| orbit-altitude | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: Cartesian position radius; orbits.test.ts: extrema and quadrature |

| photon-energy | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: frequency conversion, including rounded display |

| planck-band-radiance | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: frequency midpoint integration, all 96 scenarios |
| planck-band-photons | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: independent photon mode occupancy integral, all 96 scenarios |
| carnot-cop | confirmed | claims-audit.test.ts: reversible entropy and energy ledger |

| ideal-scan-reflection | fixed | scan-optics.test.ts: plane intersections, reciprocity, angular doubling |

## Narrative and component text

Narration retains the scoped references and drawing assumptions of its owning cards. Lesson references apply to their beats. Scene titles and scale descriptions are UI/illustration labels. No source is inferred from a numerical match alone.

| content.SCENES.1.intro | An observing spacecraft is a collection of working systems: structure holds the instrument, arrays and batteries feed it, sensors and wheels point it, computers move its data, and radiators reject heat. This cutaway uses representative geometry; the engineering examples and specifications are explicitly those of the public GOES-R civil spacecraft. | confirmed: Scene satellite: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.1.scale | Spacecraft systems · representative cutaway | confirmed: Scene satellite: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.2.title | The payload | confirmed: Scene payload: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.2.intro | Start with a complete instrument: sensor assembly, instrument electronics chassis and separate cooler controls. Open the enclosures to follow their boards and functions. ABI supplies the named civil packaging example; the drawing is representative. Component stops identify details and connections within that instrument, not an independent box for every function or company. | confirmed: Scene payload: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.2.scale | Optics, electronics and cooling · representative cutaway | confirmed: Scene payload: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.3.title | The focal plane | confirmed: Scene focal-plane: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.3.intro | A detector package is an optical surface, an electronic assembly, and a thermal load at once. This open teaching assembly separates its cold detector and readout from the warm video electronics. ABI provides the cited civil example; geometry and packaging remain representative. | confirmed: Scene focal-plane: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |
| content.SCENES.3.scale | Detector package · open teaching assembly | confirmed: Scene focal-plane: corresponding card and component references in the registry; look-model for the drawing |

| content.PARTS.orbits.3.body | The elongated guide introduces a highly elliptical orbit. Its shape and enlarged spacecraft marker are schematic. | content.PARTS.orbits.4.kicker | An intermediate orbit family | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Medium Earth Orbit; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS.orbits.5.title; content.PARTS_DATA.orbits.5.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.5.title | Low Earth orbit spacecraft | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Low Earth Orbit, Terra sun-synchronous example; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS.satellite.0.title | Infrared instrument and mounting platform | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 2-1 / PDF p. 23; Structures, printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.0.kicker | Keep the payload looking outward | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 2-1 / PDF p. 23; Structures, printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.0.body | The telescope needs an open optical port and a stable mechanical reference. On GOES-R, ABI and GLM share an Earth-pointing platform with the star trackers and inertial reference units. Their common mounting structure connects the instrument’s viewing direction to the spacecraft’s knowledge of its orientation. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 2-1 / PDF p. 23; Structures, printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.0.components.0.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.0.components.0.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.0.components.0.title | Earth Pointing Platform (EPP) | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170, Structures; printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159 |
| content.PARTS.satellite.0.components.0.body; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.0.components.0.body; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.0.components.0.body | The EPP provides the mechanical reference shared by ABI, GLM, and attitude-reference sensors. Instrument mounting and attitude knowledge therefore meet at a common structure. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170, Structures; printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159 |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.title | Spacecraft bus and equipment panels | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Structures, printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170; Figures 15-15 and 15-16; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.kicker | Carry the loads and hold alignment | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Structures, printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170; Figures 15-15 and 15-16; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.body | The bus is the load-bearing skeleton around the equipment. GOES-R uses a honeycomb-panel core around the propulsion system, a launch-vehicle adapter ring, equipment panels, and separate instrument platforms. The cutaway exposes those structural roles: mounts and decks carry the boxes; the foil-like thermal blanket is a different component. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Structures, printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170; Figures 15-15 and 15-16; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.components.0.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.components.0.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.components.0.title | Core structure and adapter ring | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170, Structures |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.components.0.body; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.components.0.body; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.components.0.body | The core structure supports the propulsion system and connects the vehicle to its launch interface. It is distinct from the instrument-support platform. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170, Structures |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.components.1.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.components.1.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.components.1.title | Equipment panels | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170, Structures; printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157 |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.components.1.body; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.components.1.body; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.components.1.body | Equipment panels provide mounting surfaces for spacecraft and instrument electronics while participating in heat transport. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170, Structures; printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157 |
| content.PARTS.satellite.1.components.2.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.components.2.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.components.2.title | EPP Launch Lock Assemblies | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 15-9 / PDF p. 169, Earth Pointing Platform Uncaging |

After release, the platform is supported by its damped isolation system. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 15-9 / PDF p. 169, Earth Pointing Platform Uncaging |

Flexible harnesses and blankets crossing the interface are part of the mechanical integration. | confirmed: nasa-goes-dual-isolation-2019: PDF pp. 2–4, GN&C Design Approach and EPP/RWA Isolation Design |

| content.PARTS.satellite.2.title | Solar array | confirmed: nasa-spacecraft-power: Section 3.2.1 Solar Cells, opening paragraphs; incidence and multi-junction cells; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, paragraph above Figure 11-3; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.kicker | Make electricity at the cells | confirmed: nasa-spacecraft-power: Section 3.2.1 Solar Cells, opening paragraphs; incidence and multi-junction cells; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, paragraph above Figure 11-3; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.body | Light absorbed in a photovoltaic semiconductor produces electrical current. Multi-junction cells stack materials that respond to different parts of the solar spectrum. GOES-R connects cells in series strings, then joins strings in parallel circuits; the thin interconnects turn a tiled surface into an electrical network. | confirmed: nasa-spacecraft-power: Section 3.2.1 Solar Cells, opening paragraphs; incidence and multi-junction cells; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, paragraph above Figure 11-3; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.components.0.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.components.0.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.components.0.title | Photovoltaic cells | confirmed: nasa-spacecraft-power: Section 3.2.1 Solar Cells, opening paragraphs; incidence and multi-junction cells |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.components.0.body; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.components.0.body; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.components.0.body | A semiconductor photovoltaic cell converts absorbed light into electrical energy. NASA describes multi-junction cells as stacked junctions that respond to different portions of the solar spectrum. | confirmed: nasa-spacecraft-power: Section 3.2.1 Solar Cells, opening paragraphs; incidence and multi-junction cells |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.components.1.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.components.1.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.components.1.title | Solar cells, strings, and circuits | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, Solar Array |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.components.1.body; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.components.1.body; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.components.1.body | GOES-R connects cells in series strings, places strings in parallel within each circuit, and connects separate circuits to the PRU. The model illustrates this electrical hierarchy without reproducing the published cell counts. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, Solar Array |
| content.PARTS.satellite.2.components.2.title; content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.components.2.title; content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.components.2.title | String and circuit isolation diodes | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, Solar Array |

| content.PARTS.satellite.4.body | The payload needs a controlled electrical supply while array output and equipment demand change. The regulator and distribution boards are separate from the light-collecting telescope. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-2 / PDF p. 134; PRU module list, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137; goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit and Fuse Board Assemblies, printed pp. 11-5–11-6 / PDF pp. 137–138; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS.satellite.5.body | The array cannot generate solar power when Earth blocks the Sun. Back in sunlight, available array power supplies the loads and recharges the batteries. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed pp. 11-2–11-4 / PDF pp. 134–136, Batteries and EPS operation; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS.satellite.11.body | A spacecraft surface is part of its thermal design. GOES-R uses radiator finishes that absorb little sunlight while efficiently emitting thermal radiation. | content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.0.body | ABI’s focal planes supply analog signals to its video electronics. The Sensor Unit Electronics digitizes the data; the Electronics Unit formats and packetizes it, then sends it through the spacecraft interface. The spacecraft computer receives an instrument data stream, rather than reading individual detector contacts itself. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Focal Plane Modules, printed p. 3-9 / PDF p. 37, first paragraph; goes-r-databook: Electronics, printed p. 3-15 / PDF p. 43; analog input described on printed p. 3-9 / PDF p. 37; goes-r-databook: Table 3-6, printed p. 3-17 / PDF p. 45, Data Processor and High Speed I/O rows; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.kicker | Connect boxes through remote interfaces | confirmed: goes-r-databook: RIU/SIU, printed pp. 10-4–10-6 / PDF pp. 128–130; common functions and operational features; goes-r-databook: Structures, printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170; Figures 15-15 and 15-16; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.1.body | The internal harness joins equipment distributed across the bus. GOES-R remote interface units receive commands, collect telemetry, and provide local electrical interfaces for relays, heaters, motors, and other equipment. The bus structure supports these boxes and routes; an electrical data bus is the communication path between them. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: RIU/SIU, printed pp. 10-4–10-6 / PDF pp. 128–130; common functions and operational features; goes-r-databook: Structures, printed pp. 15-9–15-10 / PDF pp. 169–170; Figures 15-15 and 15-16; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.kicker | Array telemetry and isolation | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.2.body | The regulator measures array current and reports it to the onboard computer. On GOES-R, separately connected array circuits and isolation diodes limit how a shorted string or circuit affects the rest of the network. The engineering record combines electrical output with the state of the power hardware. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.3.kicker | Drive electronics and resolver | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array Drive/Slip Ring Assembly, printed p. 15-4 / PDF p. 164; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.3.body | GOES-R’s solar-array drive is operated through software and dedicated drive electronics. Motors provide rotation and resolver circuits provide the position reference. The slip rings preserve the power path as the joint turns, so mechanical orientation and electrical continuity are handled together. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array Drive/Slip Ring Assembly, printed p. 15-4 / PDF p. 164; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.4.title | Power regulation and distribution unit | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit and Fuse Board Assemblies, printed pp. 11-5–11-6 / PDF pp. 137–138; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.4.body | GOES-R’s power regulator reports module temperatures, operating status, and array, battery, and load currents. Commands set the battery charge rate and operate module and load switches. Those measurements let the flight software manage supply and demand instead of treating the solar array as an uncontrolled wire to every instrument. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit and Fuse Board Assemblies, printed pp. 11-5–11-6 / PDF pp. 137–138; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.5.title | Rechargeable battery assembly | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136, charge-control paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.5.kicker | Control charging at the cell banks | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136, charge-control paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.5.body | GOES-R flight software monitors the battery’s cell-bank voltages and charge state. Charging begins with controlled current, tapers near the voltage limit, and finishes by balancing the cell banks. The battery package therefore needs sensing and control connections as well as its main power leads. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136, charge-control paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.6.kicker | Measured attitude and angular motion | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Guidance Navigation & Control, printed p. 12-1 / PDF p. 141, attitude-determination paragraph; goes-r-databook: Sun Sensors, printed pp. 12-2–12-3 / PDF pp. 142–143; goes-r-databook: On Board Computer, printed p. 10-3 / PDF p. 127; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.6.body | GOES-R combines star-tracker attitude measurements with inertial measurements for attitude determination. Sun-sensor outputs support Sun acquisition, while the computer also handles gimbal pointing. The sensors feed the estimate; the controller uses that estimate to command the actuators. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Guidance Navigation & Control, printed p. 12-1 / PDF p. 141, attitude-determination paragraph; goes-r-databook: Sun Sensors, printed pp. 12-2–12-3 / PDF pp. 142–143; goes-r-databook: On Board Computer, printed p. 10-3 / PDF p. 127; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.7.body | A reaction wheel is a commanded actuator, not an attitude sensor. GOES-R’s remote interface units provide its wheel command and telemetry interfaces. The attitude-control system uses wheels for routine body control and calls on propulsion for momentum management. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: RIU/SIU, printed pp. 10-4–10-6 / PDF pp. 128–130; common functions and operational features; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 12-1 / PDF p. 141; Propulsion Subsystem, printed p. 13-1 / PDF p. 151; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.9.body | GOES-R’s command processor validates uplink commands and gathers health telemetry, while its onboard computer routes instrument data. In the general NASA architecture, memory also holds command sequences and can retain data until transmission is available. These are distinct jobs: commanding an action, describing equipment health, and preserving an observation. Fault protection coordinates recovery across the power, attitude, thermal and communications systems. A safe state is an operating condition, not another hardware box. Radiation assurance evaluates the mission environment and electronics rather than assigning a universal radiation-proof label. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Command and Telemetry Processor, printed p. 10-2 / PDF p. 126; goes-r-databook: On Board Computer, printed p. 10-3 / PDF p. 127; nasa-onboard-data: Sequence Storage; Spacecraft Clock; Telemetry Packaging and Coding; Data Storage; Assumed: look-model; nasa-swehb-fault-detection-d: Section 3.1 ARC, 3.7.4.3; section 3.3 JPL, 4.9.2.2; nasa-swehb-fault-detection-d: Section 3.3 JPL, 4.9.1.4 and rationale; ecss-rha-2025-scope: Scope, first paragraph |

| content.PARTS_DATA.satellite.10.body | Tracking, telemetry and command—TT&C—keeps the ground connected to the spacecraft’s state and commanded actions. GOES-R’s raw instrument-data link carries observations collected by the onboard computer. Its rebroadcast service has another role again: relaying processed civil data products back to users. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Communications Subsystem, printed pp. 9-1–9-3 / PDF pp. 117–119; distinct service functions; goes-r-databook: On Board Computer, printed p. 10-3 / PDF p. 127; Assumed: look-model |

Bias establishes the electrical operating conditions; timing determines when the arrays are read. The detector’s physical arrangement and the outgoing sample stream are different descriptions of the same measurement chain. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Sensor Unit Electronics, printed p. 3-16 / PDF p. 44; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.payload.9.body | ABI’s controller computer and Telemetry and Timing card share the Electronics Unit chassis with data, power and scanner-control cards. The Peripheral and Thermal Control card is in the Sensor Unit Electronics and receives commands from the EU timing card. One coordinated instrument can therefore span several housings without making every function a separate box. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Table 3-6, printed p. 3-17 / PDF p. 45, Instrument Controller row; goes-r-databook: Table 3-6, printed p. 3-17 / PDF p. 45, Telemetry and Timing row; goes-r-databook: Sensor Unit Electronics, printed p. 3-16 / PDF p. 44, P&TC paragraph; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.payload.9.assembly.body | A common electronics chassis houses coordinated controller, data, timing, power, scan-drive and encoder-processing cards. In ABI this is the Electronics Unit, the main electrical interface to the spacecraft. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Table 3-6, printed p. 3-17 / PDF p. 45, Instrument Controller row; goes-r-databook: Table 3-6, printed p. 3-17 / PDF p. 45, Telemetry and Timing row; goes-r-databook: Sensor Unit Electronics, printed p. 3-16 / PDF p. 44, P&TC paragraph; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_DATA.focal-plane.0.body | ABI defines the focal-plane array for each spectral channel as a detector array and associated ROIC. The focal-plane module groups the arrays and filters for a spectral region. This is where detector outputs become an organized electrical readout. The larger board beside the cold plate represents later video processing, not a second detector array. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 3-9 / PDF p. 37, Focal Plane Modules and Aft Optics; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.1.kicker | Turn light into electrical power | confirmed: Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.1.body | Solar arrays convert sunlight into electrical power for the spacecraft and its instruments. Electronics also produce heat during operation. The displayed paths separate electrical supply from heat flow without assigning an operating power budget. | confirmed: Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.2.title | Spacecraft radiator | confirmed: Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.2.kicker | The thermal path | confirmed: Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.2.body | A radiator releases heat as thermal radiation. The outgoing paths represent heat leaving the spacecraft. Their appearance does not specify radiator area, heat-rejection power, or instrument temperature. | confirmed: Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.3.kicker | The spacecraft carries its power and thermal systems | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Medium Earth Orbit, Molniya discussion; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.3.body | The elongated guide introduces a highly elliptical orbit. Its shape and enlarged spacecraft marker are schematic. NASA describes Molniya as an elliptical orbit; the drawn ellipse does not encode a real trajectory. Solar arrays, batteries and heat-rejection hardware travel with the vehicle. Their detailed components can be explored at the satellite level. The orbital drawing does not simulate eclipse duration, array generation or temperature. | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Medium Earth Orbit, Molniya discussion; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.4.kicker | The spacecraft carries its power and thermal systems | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Medium Earth Orbit; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.4.body | This marker separates the medium Earth orbit family from GEO and LEO. The guide is compressed to fit this teaching view; its drawn radius is not an altitude specification. Solar arrays, batteries and heat-rejection hardware travel with the vehicle. Their detailed components can be explored at the satellite level. The orbital drawing does not simulate eclipse duration, array generation or temperature. | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Medium Earth Orbit; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.5.kicker | The spacecraft carries its power and thermal systems | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Low Earth Orbit, Terra sun-synchronous example; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.orbits.5.body | The inner guide introduces low Earth orbit. NASA describes Terra as a civil example in this family. The oversized marker is a representative spacecraft, with no mission coverage or viewing footprint assigned. Solar arrays, batteries and heat-rejection hardware travel with the vehicle. Their detailed components can be explored at the satellite level. The orbital drawing does not simulate eclipse duration, array generation or temperature. | confirmed: nasa-orbit-catalog: Low Earth Orbit, Terra sun-synchronous example; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.0.title | Infrared instrument and mounting platform | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Earth Pointing Platform, printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.0.kicker | Choose the heat paths at the mounts | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Earth Pointing Platform, printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.0.body | An instrument mount must support the payload without forcing every component to the same temperature. GOES-R mounts ABI and GLM through titanium feet and uses blankets to reduce unwanted exchange. ABI carries its own cooler and radiator path, while its Electronics Unit rejects heat through equipment panels inside the spacecraft. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Earth Pointing Platform, printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.title | Spacecraft bus and equipment panels | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.kicker | Make the deck part of the thermal system | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.1.body | GOES-R’s equipment panels do more than hold boxes: heat pipes spread heat through the panels toward radiating surfaces. Thermally conductive mounting improves the path from selected boxes to those panels. MLI and low-conductivity stand-offs reduce heat flow where an interface needs isolation instead. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.title | Solar array | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, paragraph above Figure 11-3; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-2 / PDF p. 134; PRU module list, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.kicker | Follow solar power onto the bus | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, paragraph above Figure 11-3; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-2 / PDF p. 134; PRU module list, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.2.body | The solar wing is the primary electrical source. GOES-R’s cells form series strings and parallel circuits that feed the power regulator; isolation diodes protect the common supply from a circuit fault. The amount generated depends on illumination, while the regulator determines how that available power reaches the loads. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135, paragraph above Figure 11-3; goes-r-databook: Solar Array, printed p. 11-3 / PDF p. 135; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-2 / PDF p. 134; PRU module list, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.3.kicker | Keep a moving joint within its temperature range | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array Wing Assembly, printed p. 14-6 / PDF p. 160; goes-r-databook: Solar Array Drive/Slip Ring Assembly, printed p. 15-4 / PDF p. 164; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.3.body | A drive assembly combines mechanical motion with an electrical interface. GOES-R blankets its gimbals while leaving their rotation interfaces clear and uses heaters for thermal control. The drive must rotate the wing and maintain its power connection across changing thermal conditions. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Solar Array Wing Assembly, printed p. 14-6 / PDF p. 160; goes-r-databook: Solar Array Drive/Slip Ring Assembly, printed p. 15-4 / PDF p. 164; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.4.body | GOES-R uses switched array shunts to regulate its main bus. Battery charger/dischargers use buck/boost conversion to move power in either direction, and buck converters create the lower-voltage supply. Protected distribution switches and fuses then divide those supplies among the spacecraft loads. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Electrical Power Subsystem, printed pp. 11-1–11-2 / PDF pp. 133–134; nominal bus names, not generic spacecraft voltages; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 11-2 / PDF p. 134; PRU module list, printed p. 11-5 / PDF p. 137; goes-r-databook: Power Regulation Unit and Fuse Board Assemblies, printed pp. 11-5–11-6 / PDF pp. 137–138; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.5.title | Rechargeable battery assembly | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136; printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136, charge-control paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.5.kicker | Remove discharge heat and add heat when needed | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136; printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136, charge-control paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.5.body | A battery needs its own thermal path. GOES-R uses temperature sensors and heaters in the battery package and dedicated radiators to reject discharge heat. Electrical charge control and temperature control work alongside one another; neither is supplied by the solar cells alone. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136; printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, final paragraph; goes-r-databook: Batteries, printed p. 11-4 / PDF p. 136, charge-control paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.6.kicker | Stabilize the sensor mounting environment | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 2-1 / PDF p. 23; Structures, printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170; goes-r-databook: Earth Pointing Platform, printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.6.body | GOES-R’s Earth-pointing platform co-locates the instruments and attitude-reference hardware. Its star tracker has a dedicated radiator, thermal straps, and heaters, while the inertial units use a cold-plate/radiator assembly. Thermal control is part of maintaining the measurement environment, not just protecting electronics from damage. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 2-1 / PDF p. 23; Structures, printed p. 15-10 / PDF p. 170; goes-r-databook: Earth Pointing Platform, printed p. 14-5 / PDF p. 159; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.7.kicker | Give motorized equipment a rejection path | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 12-1 / PDF p. 141; Propulsion Subsystem, printed p. 13-1 / PDF p. 151; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.7.body | GOES-R mounts reaction-wheel assemblies on thermally controlled equipment panels along with computers and communications hardware. The panel carries their heat toward radiating surfaces. A wheel’s mechanical job is attitude control; its mounting also supplies structural support and a thermal interface. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; goes-r-databook: Printed p. 12-1 / PDF p. 141; Propulsion Subsystem, printed p. 13-1 / PDF p. 151; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.8.body | GOES-R’s MLI-lined bus cavity moderates the environment around propulsion components. Thruster-heater interfaces support temperature control, and a heat shield protects nearby hardware around the apogee engine. The tank, feed line, actuator, and exhaust region impose different thermal needs. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, MLI and LAE paragraph; goes-r-databook: RIU/SIU, printed pp. 10-4–10-6 / PDF pp. 128–130; common functions and operational features; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.9.body | The flight computer and other electronics occupy boxes attached to GOES-R’s thermally controlled equipment panels. Where more conductance is needed, the mounting uses a thermally conductive bond. The chassis and its contact with the panel are therefore part of the heat path, alongside the circuitry’s electrical connections. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; Assumed: look-model; nasa-swehb-fault-detection-d: Section 3.1 ARC, 3.7.4.3; section 3.3 JPL, 4.9.2.2; nasa-swehb-fault-detection-d: Section 3.3 JPL, 4.9.1.4 and rationale; ecss-rha-2025-scope: Scope, first paragraph |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.10.body | GOES-R’s communications electronics share thermally controlled equipment panels. Its antenna horns use RF-transparent sunshield blankets, and its steerable reflector is also blanketed. Thermal surfaces must manage sunlight while preserving the antenna’s communications function. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Printed p. 14-3 / PDF p. 157, equipment-panel radiators and wet/dry mounting paragraphs; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.11.kicker | Spread heat before radiating it | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; Assumed: look-model |
| content.PARTS_HEAT.satellite.11.body | GOES-R embeds heat pipes in radiator panels to spread heat and reduce hot spots. Optical solar reflectors combine low solar absorption with strong thermal emission. Heat flows through the mounting and transport hardware to the panel, then leaves the spacecraft as radiation. | confirmed: goes-r-databook: Passive thermal control, printed p. 14-2 / PDF p. 156; Assumed: look-model |

| content.PARTS_HEAT.payload.1.body | ABI’s scan shrouds protect the internal instrument structure when solar energy enters the optical port. | lesson:pixel.title | See light become data | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.0.title | A photon reaches the absorber | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.0.body | An absorbed photon can create mobile charge carriers. Some incoming light does not produce collected charge. | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.1.title | The electric field collects charge | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.1.body | Electron and hole motion creates a measurable electrical response. The enlarged dots represent carriers, not data packets. | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.2.title | Charge becomes a voltage | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.2.body | An ideal integration capacitance accumulates the signal. More collected charge changes the voltage; the graph shows its magnitude. | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.3.title | The converter makes a digital sample | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.3.body | Later analog-to-digital conversion assigns the measured voltage to a numerical bin. The enlarged bins are only a teaching example. | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.4.title | A sample takes its place in an image | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pixel.beats.4.body | Many spatial samples form an image. The highlighted cell follows this one signal; the surrounding image is synthetic. | confirmed: cinematic:detector; cinematic:charge; cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.title | See how the detector stays cold | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.0.title | The detector is a heat load | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.0.body | The cold assembly receives heat from its surroundings and its own electronics. Cold does not mean no heat is flowing. | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.1.title | The cold finger carries heat away | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.1.body | A conductive connection carries heat from the detector toward the cold end of the cooler. | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.2.title | Electrical work drives the cooler | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.2.body | The cooler moves heat toward a warmer rejection interface. Electricity and heat are different flows. | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.3.title | The warm side rejects more heat | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.3.body | Heat leaving the cooler equals the heat it removed plus the electrical work it consumed, over a steady cycle. | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.4.title | The radiator emits to space | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:cooling.beats.4.body | Conduction brings heat to a radiating surface. Thermal radiation carries energy away; there is no outside cooling airflow in vacuum. | confirmed: cinematic:cooling; cinematic:radiator; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.title | See how the spacecraft turns | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.0.title | Start with a fixed star reference | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.0.body | The starfield stays fixed while the schematic body and its internal wheel turn. This is attitude change, not a change in orbital path. | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.1.title | The motor accelerates the wheel | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.1.body | A torque on the wheel produces an opposite torque on the spacecraft. Both motions follow the same momentum calculation. | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.2.title | The body turns in the other direction | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.2.body | The smaller wheel spins through a larger angle. Its motion relative to the body differs from its motion relative to the stars. | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.3.title | Reverse the torque to brake | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.3.body | Slowing the wheel brings this ideal spacecraft to rest at its new orientation. The body does not turn backward to stop. | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.4.title | Hold the new pointing direction | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:wheel.beats.4.body | Both start and finish at rest in this example. Real spacecraft also manage external torques and periodically unload accumulated momentum. | confirmed: cinematic:wheel; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.title | See an image being built | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.0.title | A landscape passes beneath the sensor | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.0.body | This invented river and fields give you features to follow. The drawing explains the Landsat pushbroom principle, not an actual overpass. | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.1.title | One line spans the image swath | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.1.body | A row of detectors samples across the direction of travel. Spacecraft motion brings successive strips into view. | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.2.title | Successive lines build the image | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.2.body | The moving sample line and the growing image use exactly the same synthetic landscape values. | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.3.title | The river appears in the assembled data | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.3.body | Across-track position comes from the detector row; along-track position comes from successive observations. | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.4.title | Many lines become one spatial picture | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:pushbroom.beats.4.body | The drawing uses an enlarged sampling grid. Real products also need calibration and geometric processing. | confirmed: cinematic:pushbroom; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.title | See why GEO stays overhead | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.0.title | Watch Earth and satellite from space | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.0.body | An ideal geostationary satellite circles in the equatorial plane, in the same direction and with the same period as Earth rotates. | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.1.title | Follow one longitude | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.1.body | The highlighted ground marker turns with Earth. The satellite remains aligned with it while both move against the stars. | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.2.title | Change to the rotating frame | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.2.body | The main view now turns with Earth. The inset keeps the original space-fixed view so the two descriptions stay connected. | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.3.title | The satellite stays over one place | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.3.body | In the Earth-rotating view, both marker and satellite are fixed. Geosynchronous orbits with inclination or eccentricity need not stay overhead. | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.4.title | Stillness depends on your viewpoint | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:geo.beats.4.body | The orbit has not stopped. Only the reference frame changed. Sizes and spacing are compressed for this diagram. | confirmed: cinematic:geo; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.title | See power through an eclipse | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.0.title | Sunlight supplies the load | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.0.body | The solar array supplies electrical power. The battery begins charged; all chart values are normalized teaching quantities. | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.1.title | The spacecraft enters Earth’s shadow | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.1.body | Solar input disappears during the illustrated eclipse. The battery begins supplying the same electrical load. | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.2.title | Stored energy falls as the load runs | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.2.body | Battery energy falls by the energy delivered. This ideal balance omits losses and does not represent a mission eclipse duration. | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.3.title | Sunlight returns and recharges the battery | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.3.body | The array supplies the load and a charging surplus. Energy flows into the battery, and the stored-energy trace rises. | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.4.title | The energy budget closes | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:eclipse.beats.4.body | The teaching cycle restores the starting charge. Real sizing must account for efficiency, degradation, thermal limits and the actual orbit. | confirmed: cinematic:power; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.title | See the image arrive on Earth | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.0.title | Begin with an already digital image | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.0.body | A synthetic river image is held in memory. Digitization happened earlier in the payload electronics. | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.1.title | Group the samples into packets | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.1.body | The highlighted image rows become labeled data groups. Packet size and ordering here are drawing choices. | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.2.title | Transmit the encoded data | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.2.body | A radio link carries a modulated electromagnetic signal. Moving packet symbols track information, not physical boxes flying through space. | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.3.title | Receive and reconstruct the image | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.3.body | The receiver recovers data; successive rows appear in the same positions as the source image. No link rate or error performance is implied. | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.4.title | The same river reaches the ground | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:downlink.beats.4.body | Recognizable features survive the complete path. Reception, image processing and any later interpretation are separate jobs. | confirmed: cinematic:conversion; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.title | See heat as light | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.0.title | A warm object radiates | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.0.body | This ideal blackbody is a teaching source. The colors reveal infrared radiation that a human eye cannot see. | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.1.title | Raise the temperature | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.1.body | Increasing the assumed temperature raises the emitted spectral radiance. The curve is calculated with Planck’s law. | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.2.title | The peak shifts toward shorter wavelengths | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.2.body | The axis is wavelength, increasing to the right. The same fixed vertical scale is used throughout the comparison. | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.3.title | Compare two thermal spectra | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.3.body | The original curve remains as a dim reference. The brighter curve shows the hotter ideal source. | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.4.title | A real plume has additional spectral structure | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:thermal.beats.4.body | Molecular gases add wavelength-dependent emission. This smooth blackbody example is not a plume spectrum or a detection model. | confirmed: cinematic:spectrum; cinematic:molecular; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.title | See the atmosphere change the light | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.0.title | Light enters a layer of air | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.0.body | Start with an ideal thermal spectrum. The slab and its smooth absorption features are invented teaching inputs. | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.1.title | Some wavelengths transmit more readily | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.1.body | The transmission curve changes the shape of the incoming spectrum. This diagram gives no real atmospheric window or observation condition. | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.2.title | The atmosphere also emits | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.2.body | A warm medium contributes its own radiation. Emission is not a packet of absorbed light immediately continuing down the same path. | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.3.title | Add the two contributions | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.3.body | Outgoing radiance combines transmitted source light with the slab’s thermal emission. The colored curves use the same radiance scale. | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.4.title | What arrives includes the path itself | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:atmosphere.beats.4.body | A measurement depends on the source and the intervening medium. This ideal non-scattering, isothermal model is a first-principles example. | confirmed: cinematic:atmosphere; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.title | See how calibration works | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.0.title | A detector reading has an offset and gain | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.0.body | The synthetic image contains an intentionally injected brightness error. The scene itself has not changed. | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.1.title | The mirror selects a reference view | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.1.body | TIRS-2 can select Earth, an onboard blackbody and space. The moving mirror here indicates selection, not its optical prescription. | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.2.title | Measure distinct reference signals | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.2.body | Two known teaching references reveal an ideal linear response. In a real instrument, reference radiance and thermal conditions must be characterized. | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.3.title | Apply the fitted correction | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.3.body | The same two-point equation corrects the synthetic data. The split image shows the injected error and the corrected result. | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.4.title | Return to Earth with a calibrated response | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |
| lesson:calibration.beats.4.body | This example removes only its own gain and offset. Noise, nonlinearity and other errors require more than this demonstration. | confirmed: cinematic:references; cinematic:calibration; cinematic-presentation; cinematic-model-inputs |

## Teaching assumptions and limits

| ID | Value | Footnote |
|---|---|---|
| cinematic-presentation | Representative geometry, synthetic images and illustrative playback | footnoted: These are explanatory diagrams, not fabrication drawings or operational simulations. Enlarged carriers, rays, packets, colors, time, camera travel and sampling grids serve readability. No detector format, performance, mission timeline, orbit slot or real site is specified. |
| cinematic-model-inputs | Normalized charge, voltage, energy, radiance and inertia | footnoted: The detector example uses efficiency 0.65, capacitance 1 and eight illustrative quantization bins. The wheel example uses bus/wheel inertias 12:1 and a 1.2-radian teaching turn. Power uses load 1, sunlight supply 1 or 2 and eclipse supply 0. The cooler balance uses heat removed 1 and work input 2, so heat rejected is 3 in matching arbitrary units; these are not cooler capabilities. These arbitrary values show equations, not instrument specifications. The atmosphere uses an invented smooth transmission curve and an isothermal non-scattering slab. Calibration uses gain 1.15 and offset 0.15 in normalized units, without noise or spectral response. |
| illustration-orbit-motion | Compressed drawing geometry and an illustration clock | footnoted: Orbit guides retain their authored drawing dimensions and shapes. Motion follows each guide’s own ellipse or circle. The physical teaching orbit calculations are separate: no real constellation state, observation geometry, or operational schedule is inferred from this animation. |
| cooler-cycle-boundary | Complete cycle or steady average; no net stored energy | footnoted: The symbolic balance treats the cooler as a closed cyclic device with heat absorbed, input work, and rejected heat. It assigns no numerical load, efficiency, temperature, or rate to a spacecraft. Startup, cooldown, and other transients would require a stored-energy term. |
| model-orbits | A spherical Earth and negligible satellite mass | footnoted: The sphere uses the published equatorial radius, 6,378.137 km. GEO uses a 35,786 km circular reference altitude. HEO is a teaching ellipse with period one half of the published sidereal day and eccentricity 0.722, evaluated at apogee. MEO and LEO are arbitrary circular examples at 20,000 km and 1,000 km. These are not program or spacecraft orbital parameters, and no constellation is computed. |
| model-nadir | The surface point directly below the illustrated orbit position | footnoted: The central angle is zero. This keeps the distance and light-time example simple without assuming a real observing direction or ground station. HEO uses the apogee position. |
| model-lab-aperture | 0.30 m unobstructed circular diameter | footnoted: An arbitrary mathematical example used only for diffraction. It is not the aperture of any depicted military hardware or civil instrument. The civil aperture selection returns unavailable because the ABI diameter has not been verified. |
| model-band-examples | SWIR: 2.0 μm, interval 1.5–2.5 μm; MWIR: 4.3 μm, interval 3.8–4.8 μm; LWIR: 10.0 μm, interval 8–12 μm | footnoted: These illustrative wavelengths and top-hat integration bounds are chosen to compare the equations. They are not formal definitions of the broad infrared band names and are not any instrument’s spectral response or atmospheric transmission windows. |
| model-blackbody | 288 K, emissivity 1 | footnoted: A uniform ideal blackbody provides an elementary radiance example. It is not a measured Earth scene, plume, satellite background, or detector background. Orbit, aperture and detector choices do not affect this source radiance. |
| look-model | Representative / not to scale | footnoted: The prototype’s geometry, layout, satellite counts and positions, and ray paths are chosen to explain component roles. They do not describe a real constellation, sensor performance, or physical dimensions. |

## Built-page numeric and because inventory

The page inventory includes source locators and UI metadata, not just physics. Registered values are checked above; inline source citations and method formulas carry their own references. The checked-in review manifest classifies exact bibliographic metadata, UI counters, dates, shortcuts and instrument names as ui-label, separately from confirmed physical claims and footnoted teaching assumptions. These records are deliberate review decisions, not generated approvals. Unknown or changed text, context, links or evidence keys fail the audit. Repeated visible copies remain listed. To update a record, inspect the changed sentence and supporting source/test first; never regenerate approvals from page text alone.

| visualizer | The ideal surface is z = (x² + y²)/(4f). Each ray reflects using d′ = d − 2(d·n)n and reaches (0, 0, f). Equal path lengths from the entry plane give equal arrival times at the focus. |  | confirmed: ideal-prime-focus: ideal-focus.test.ts independently checks reflected focus direction and equal optical paths; NASA Basics of Space Flight chapter 6 Reflection. Surface and on-axis incoming rays are ideal assumptions. |
| visualizer | Calc. reflection uses the same vector law at each planar surface; ray intersections are solved with plane equations. For a fixed ray and a single plane of rotation, the reflected direction changes by twice the mirror angle. Incoming light follows the solved path in reverse (optical reciprocity). Assumed mirror spacing, apertures, angles, screen, trail, and playback are drawing choices. The screen shows viewing directions, not a ground footprint, detector image, or scan schedule. The feedback animation illustrates roles without a servo-response model. The public civil ABI uses scan-mirror drives and optical encoder electronics: NOAA GOES-R Data Book, Table 3-6. This diagram is not its optical layout. |  | footnoted: ideal-scan-reflection: scan-optics.test.ts plane intersections, reciprocity and double-angle checks; NASA reflection principle. ABI motor/encoder roles: NOAA GOES-R Data Book Table 3-6, printed 3-17/PDF45. All drawn spacing/angles/servo motion explicitly assumed. |

| method | Bλ = 2hc² / [λ⁵(exp(hc/(λkT))−1)], evaluated with the existing SI Planck model. The thermal lesson compares assumed 400 K and up to 800 K ideal blackbodies over 1–20 micrometers. The atmospheric example uses assumed 500 K source and 280 K slab over the same interval. All curves share a fixed radiance normalization within each lesson. False color and ray brightness are illustrative. |  | confirmed: Exact calculation definition calc-cinematic-spectrum; independent check in calculation test map, with teaching inputs retained. |
| method | In normalized teaching units Q = ηN and positive signal magnitude ΔV = Q/C. An ideal uniform ADC clips floor(L ΔV/Vfull) to 0…L−1. In SI, Q = ηNe. The diagram does not prescribe readout polarity, CTIA topology, capacitance, bit depth, or conversion location for a real sensor. |  | confirmed: Exact calculation definition calc-cinematic-charge; independent check in calculation test map, with teaching inputs retained. |
| method | With zero external torque and initial angular momentum zero, (Ib+Iw)ωbus + Iwωwheel,relative = 0. A smooth rest-to-rest bus angle determines wheel angle and speed through this relation. | method | For a non-scattering isothermal medium in local thermodynamic equilibrium, Lout(λ) = τ(λ) Lin(λ) + [1−τ(λ)] Bλ(Tair). The diagram uses invented optical depth; it cannot describe any actual atmosphere or observation condition. Absorbed incoming energy is not assumed to be re-emitted immediately along the ray. |  | confirmed: Exact calculation definition calc-cinematic-slab; independent check in calculation test map, with teaching inputs retained. |
| method | Given two distinct known reference signals S0 and S1 and measured readings D0 and D1, Scorrected = S0 + (D−D0)(S1−S0)/(D1−D0). This teaching fit removes only the injected gain and offset; it does not solve noise, nonlinearity, stray light, atmospheric effects or real instrument calibration. |  | confirmed: Exact calculation definition calc-cinematic-calibration; independent check in calculation test map, with teaching inputs retained. |
| method | The surface z = (x² + y²)/(4f) reflects an on-axis plane wave to (0, 0, f). Each path from a common entry plane to the focus has length entry + f. The independent tests compare the reflected direction to the focus direction and verify equal path lengths. This is geometric optics; no diffraction spot or real optical prescription is computed. |  | confirmed: Exact calculation definition calc-ideal-prime-focus; independent check in calculation test map, with teaching inputs retained. |

| method | Each ray intersects a mirror plane and reflects with d′ = d − 2(d·n)n. In a single plane a mirror rotation changes the outgoing direction by twice that angle. Two successive reflections are solved as vectors, not added scalar angles. Tests check plane intersections, equal incidence/reflection angles, reciprocity, and angular doubling. Drawing dimensions and timing are illustrative; no servo response or real scan schedule is modeled. |  | confirmed: Exact calculation definition calc-ideal-scan-reflection; independent check in calculation test map, with teaching inputs retained. |

Power uses load 1, sunlight supply 1 or 2 and eclipse supply 0. | parts | The same component names and descriptions appear here and in the 3D cards. Large assemblies contain individually named subcomponents; each entry carries its evidence. Payload details are grouped under their sensor, electronics or cooler-control parent. A selectable function does not imply a separate enclosure, and a supplier responsibility does not define a physical box. GOES-R and ABI provide the detailed civil spacecraft example, while TIRS-2 shows a different instrument architecture. Shared components appear again where a close-up or civil comparison needs them. |  | footnoted: look-model and component-catalog scope: public civil component taxonomy, not an as-built military bill of materials. ## Verification and limitations

Run: npx tsc --noEmit; npx vitest run; npx tsx tools/claims.mjs; npm run build; GR_URL=<isolated preview> node tools/claim-page-inventory.mjs; npx tsx tools/claim-audit-report.mjs. The inventory scans DOM text (including expandable text) and model data, not arbitrary pixels. Browser captures cover all six pages at 360 and 1440 px. Full rendering/performance certification belongs to the separate visual/performance briefs.
